q: Bakelite, a hard thermosetting plastic, is made by condensation polymerisation of phenol with:
x: Phenol and methanal (formaldehyde) join through –CH₂– bridges with loss of water, building a cross-linked network. Ethane-1,2-diol and hexane-1,6-diamine are monomers of polyesters and nylons.

q: Nylon-6, with repeat unit –NH(CH₂)₅CO–, can be made from a single monomer. That monomer is:
x: The repeat unit holds one NH and one CO joined by five CH₂ groups, so one molecule carrying both an amino group and a carboxyl group, 6-aminohexanoic acid, condenses with itself. The diamine and the diacid together make nylon-6,6, the common mix-up.

q: Which of these polymers can be broken down by hydrolysis of the links in its main chain?
x: Nylon-6,6 is a condensation polymer whose –CO–NH– amide links can be hydrolysed by acid or alkali. The addition polymers have a backbone of C–C bonds only, which water cannot break; this is why they are not biodegradable.

q: The repeat unit of poly(propene) is:
x: In addition polymerisation the C=C of CH₂=CHCH₃ opens, so the two former double-bond carbons form the chain and CH₃ is a side group. Putting all three carbons in the chain ignores that CH₃ is a branch; keeping the double bond is wrong because it opens up.

q: Kevlar has the repeat unit –CO–C₆H₄–CO–NH–C₆H₄–NH– (both rings 1,4-substituted). Its monomers and type of polymer are:
o: Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diamine; a condensation polyester
Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diol; a condensation polyester
Phenylethene and acrylonitrile; an addition copolymer
Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diamine; a condensation polyamide
x: Cutting each –CO–NH– link and adding back H₂O gives HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH and H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂; the links are amide links, so it is a polyamide like nylon. Calling it a polyester confuses –CO–NH– with –CO–O–.

Maltose is two α-glucose units joined by a 1,4-glycosidic link, so hydrolysis gives only glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose, and glucose and galactose from lactose; these are the usual mix-ups.

q: 9.0 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (180 g mol⁻¹), is completely burnt in oxygen. What volume of CO₂ is formed at STP? (molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Moles of glucose = 9.0/180 = 0.050, so CO₂ = 0.30 mol = 0.30 × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³. Forgetting the 1 : 6 ratio gives 1.12 dm³.

q: Vegetable oils such as sunflower oil are liquids at room temperature, while animal fats such as beef fat are solids. The main reason is that the oils:
o: Contain more glycerol units per molecule
Have much higher molar masses than fats
Contain more C=C double bonds in their fatty acid chains, so the molecules pack less closely
Are made of free fatty acids rather than triglycerides
x: Both are triglycerides of glycerol. The cis double bonds in unsaturated chains put bends in them, so the molecules cannot pack tightly and the van der Waals forces are weaker, giving a lower melting point. Every triglyceride has one glycerol unit, so that option is wrong.

o: The storage polysaccharide of animals, kept in the liver and muscles
The storage polysaccharide of plants, kept in seeds and tubers
The structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls
x: Animals store glucose as glycogen, a highly branched polymer of glucose. Starch is the plant store and cellulose the plant structural material; lactose is the milk sugar.

q: Glyceryl trioleate (884 g mol⁻¹) is a triglyceride in which each of the three fatty acid chains contains one C=C bond. What mass of hydrogen is needed to saturate 88.4 g of it completely? (H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹)
x: 88.4/884 = 0.10 mol of fat; each molecule has three C=C bonds, so 0.30 mol H₂ = 0.30 × 2 = 0.6 g. Allowing only one C=C per molecule gives 0.2 g; using moles of H atoms instead of H₂ gives 0.3 g.

q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
x: RNA uses uracil in place of the thymine of DNA; adenine, guanine and cytosine are found in both. Choosing thymine reverses the two nucleic acids.

q: An enzyme usually catalyses only one reaction or one type of substrate. This is mainly because:
o: It raises the activation energy of all other reactions
It is used up in the reaction it catalyses
Its active site has a shape that fits only particular substrate molecules
x: Substrate and active site fit like a lock and key, held by specific interactions, so only matching molecules bind and react. Enzymes lower activation energy and are not consumed, so the other options contradict how catalysts work.

q: Covalent cross-links that help hold the tertiary structure of many proteins are disulfide (–S–S–) bridges. They form between the side chains of:
x: Cysteine has a –CH₂SH side chain, and two –SH groups are oxidised to an –S–S– bridge. Lysine side chains take part in ionic attractions, not covalent S–S links; glycine and alanine have no sulphur.

q: A double-stranded DNA segment has 10 base pairs, of which 4 are guanine–cytosine pairs and the rest are adenine–thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together in this segment?
x: G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs by two: 4 × 3 + 6 × 2 = 12 + 12 = 24. Giving every pair two bonds gives 20 and every pair three gives 30; swapping the counts for the two kinds of pair gives 26.

q: Which of these is a globular protein?
x: Haemoglobin is folded into a compact, roughly spherical shape and is soluble, as befits a carrier protein. Keratin (hair, nails), collagen (tendons) and silk fibroin are long, insoluble fibrous proteins with structural roles.
